questions.a: Heartbeats with TTL in a fast store, broadcasting changes only to interested peers in batches, and not showing presence for huge channels.

questions.q: How does email delivery handle failures?
questions.a: Store-and-forward queues with retries and backoff on temporary (4xx) errors for days and bounces on permanent (5xx) errors.

questions.q: What are SPF, DKIM and DMARC?
questions.a: SPF lists servers allowed to send for a domain, DKIM signs messages with the domain's key, and DMARC sets policy and reporting based on both.

questions.q: How would you design the ETA service?
questions.a: Prep time plus courier-to-restaurant plus restaurant-to-customer travel from a road graph with live traffic, corrected by a model trained on historical delivery outcomes.

questions.q: How do you handle a courier who stops sending location?
questions.a: Mark the courier stale after missed pings, alert the customer if needed, and re-dispatch the order.

questions.q: How would you detect bidding fraud?
questions.a: Pattern analysis of bidder-seller relationships, new account behaviour, bid timing and retractions, plus payment verification for high-value items.

questions.q: What does offline-first mean?
questions.a: The UI reads from a local database and writes locally first, and a sync engine reconciles with the server in the background.

questions.q: Why queue actions with client-generated ids?
questions.a: So retries after timeouts are idempotent and duplicates are ignored by the server.

questions.q: How do you sync after being offline for days?
questions.a: Use a cursor or sequence token to fetch changes in pages, apply tombstones for deletes, and fall back to a full resync if the token is too old.

questions.q: Why are tombstones needed?
questions.a: Without them an offline device cannot learn about a deletion and may push the old item back.

questions.q: How do you resolve conflicting offline edits?
questions.a: Choose by data meaning: last write wins for trivial fields, field-level three-way merge, operation-based merge for counters and lists, CRDTs for collaboration, or ask the user.

questions.q: Why can't you rely on push notifications for correctness?
questions.a: Delivery is best effort and can be delayed, dropped or throttled; the app must be able to fetch the data itself.

questions.q: How would you upload a large video from a phone?
questions.a: Resumable chunked upload directly to object storage with a pre-signed URL, verify checksums, then process asynchronously.

questions.q: What is adaptive bitrate streaming?
questions.a: Video is transcoded into several renditions and cut into short segments; the player picks a rendition each segment based on measured throughput.

questions.q: How do you design the API to support old app versions?
questions.a: Version the API, add only optional fields, ignore unknown fields, keep behaviour for minimum supported versions, use feature flags and force upgrades only as a last resort.

questions.q: How do you reduce battery drain from networking?
questions.a: Batch requests, avoid polling, use push and OS-scheduled background work, compress, and respect low-power and data-saver modes.

questions.q: How do you handle token storage and refresh on mobile?
questions.a: Store tokens in the keychain or keystore, use short-lived access tokens with rotating refresh tokens, and handle revocation gracefully.

questions.q: How do you prevent out-of-memory crashes from images?
questions.a: Request right-sized images from a resizing CDN, downsample bitmaps to view size, use bounded memory and disk caches, and avoid holding full-size decoded images.

questions.q: What metrics matter for mobile client observability?
questions.a: Startup time, frame drops, crash-free sessions, network failures by connection type, API latency from the client and battery impact.

questions.q: How do silent pushes and background sync interact?
questions.a: A data push can wake the app to sync, but the OS throttles frequency and execution time, so the app must tolerate missed or delayed wake-ups.

questions.q: What is an inverted index?
questions.a: A mapping from each term to the documents (and positions) that contain it, so queries intersect postings lists instead of scanning text.

questions.q: What is text analysis in search?
questions.a: Tokenising and normalising text (lowercase, stop words, stemming, synonyms) the same way at index and query time.

questions.q: Explain TF-IDF and BM25.
questions.a: TF rewards terms frequent in a document, IDF rewards terms rare across the corpus. BM25 adds saturating term frequency and document length normalisation with parameters k1 and b.

questions.q: How does a distributed search query execute?
questions.a: Scatter to all shards, each returns local top-k with scores, and the coordinator merges them; replicas add availability and throughput.

questions.q: Why is search eventually consistent with the primary database?
questions.a: Updates flow asynchronously through CDC or a queue and become visible after the next refresh; the database remains the source of truth.

questions.q: How would you implement autocomplete?
questions.a: A trie or edge n-gram index keyed by prefix, with candidates ranked by popularity and recency, cached and updated from query logs.

questions.q: How do you add typo tolerance?
questions.a: Fuzzy matching with edit distance via automata or n-gram candidates, phonetic algorithms for names, and query suggestions from term statistics.

questions.q: Compare multi-tenancy models.
questions.a: Shared tables with tenant_id are cheapest but need strict filtering; schema per tenant and database per tenant increase isolation and cost; cells or hybrids group tenants by size.

questions.q: Hierarchy storage patterns?
questions.a: Adjacency list (parent_id), materialised path, nested sets and closure table, trading read simplicity, subtree queries and move cost.

questions.q: How do you reindex without downtime?
questions.a: Build a new index with the new analyser in parallel, replay or backfill data, keep it updated, then switch an alias atomically.

questions.q: Why is deep pagination expensive in search?
questions.a: Each shard must compute and return all results up to the offset; use search_after cursors or cap the depth.

questions.q: How do you model time-series data?
questions.a: Partition by time, key by series and time, downsample with rollups and retention tiers, and control label cardinality.

questions.q: How do you make schema changes with no downtime?
questions.a: Expand and contract: add compatible structure, dual write, backfill in batches, switch reads, then remove the old structure.

questions.q: Soft delete trade-offs?
questions.a: Recoverability and auditing versus polluted queries, broken unique constraints (use partial indexes) and legal deletion duties; purge on a schedule or use crypto-shredding.

questions.q: Explain sharding to a non-engineer.
questions.a: Like splitting a library's books across rooms by author name: each room is smaller and faster to search, but finding things across rooms is harder and some rooms get busier.

questions.q: Explain caching in one analogy.
questions.a: Keeping the books you use most on your desk instead of walking to the library; fast, small and sometimes out of date.

questions.q: What is the difference between replication and sharding?
questions.a: Replication copies the same data to several nodes for safety and read capacity; sharding splits different data across nodes for capacity.

questions.q: Explain a load balancer.
questions.a: A host who seats each party at a table with space and stops seating at tables without a waiter.

questions.q: Explain CAP with an analogy.
questions.a: Two bank branches with a broken phone line must either refuse withdrawals until they can talk (consistent) or allow them and reconcile later (available).

questions.q: Explain consistent hashing in plain words.
questions.a: Servers and keys are placed on a circle; each key belongs to the next server clockwise, so adding a server moves only the keys between it and its neighbour.

questions.q: Why do we need idempotency?
questions.a: Retries after timeouts are unavoidable, and repeating a non-idempotent action such as payment would duplicate its effect.

questions.q: Explain a queue versus pub/sub versus a log.
questions.a: A queue gives each message to one worker, pub/sub gives it to every subscriber, a log keeps an ordered history many readers can replay.

questions.q: Why are backups needed in addition to replication?
questions.a: Replication faithfully copies mistakes such as deletes and corruption; backups give a point-in-time state to restore.

questions.q: Why is p99 more useful than the average?
questions.a: Users and fan-out requests experience the slow tail; averages hide it.

questions.q: How do you explain a trade-off to an interviewer?
questions.a: Name the pain, the tool that addresses it, what it costs, and the condition under which you would choose differently.

questions.q: When is a monolith the better choice?
questions.a: For small teams and early products where a modular monolith is simpler to build, test, deploy and debug; split into services when scale, team or release independence demand it.

questions.q: Explain eventual consistency and where it is not acceptable.
questions.a: Replicas converge if updates stop, fine for likes and feeds; unacceptable for money, inventory counts and uniqueness constraints without extra coordination.

questions.q: Give the back-of-the-envelope recipe.
questions.a: Convert users into per-second rates, rates into servers, rates times size into storage and bandwidth, and state assumptions and peak factors explicitly.
